items.stem: Define the term 'wireless local area network (WLAN)'.
items.answer: A local area network in which devices connect using radio waves (Wi-Fi) through wireless access points rather than cables.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A local area network in which devices connect using radio waves (Wi-Fi) through wireless access points rather than cables. [2]

items.stem: Explain how a VPN keeps data secure.
items.answer: It creates an encrypted tunnel between the user's device and the private network, so data sent over the internet cannot be read if intercepted; users must also authenticate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark encrypted tunnel; 1 mark intercepted data unreadable/authentication. [2]

items.stem: Explain two advantages of a WLAN for an office.
items.answer: Staff can move around with laptops; no cabling costs or disruption; easy to add devices; supports visitors and mobile devices.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Mohammed is planning the network for a new branch of Eagles Sports Club in Santiago. Describe what is meant by a WLAN.
items.answer: A local network where devices connect wirelessly through access points.
items.markingKey: 1 mark local; 1 mark wireless/access points. [2]

items.stem: Priya is planning the network for a new branch of Lakeside College in Dubai. (a) Describe what is meant by a WLAN. (b) Explain why staff working from home should use a VPN.
items.answer: (a) A local network where devices connect wirelessly through access points. (b) Encrypted tunnel protects data over the internet; access to internal resources as if in the office.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark local; 1 mark wireless/access points. [2] (b) 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: City Central Library, a library in Cape Town, has staff who work in the office, at home and while travelling. Discuss whether City Central Library should rely on a WLAN rather than a cabled network in its new branch.
items.answer: Points for: mobility; cheaper and faster installation; flexible. Points against / limitations: lower speed and reliability; interference; security risks; limited range. Conclusion: a mix — cabled for fixed workstations and servers, wireless for mobile users.

items.stem: Distinguish between 'wireless access point (WAP)' and 'virtual private network (VPN)'.
items.answer: wireless access point (WAP): A device that allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi. virtual private network (VPN): A secure, encrypted connection (tunnel) over a public network such as the internet, allowing a remote user to access a private network as if connected locally.

items.stem: Define the term 'protocol'.
items.answer: A set of rules that governs how data is formatted, transmitted and received between devices on a network.

items.stem: Explain why protocols are needed for communication on the internet.
items.answer: Devices from different manufacturers and running different software must agree on rules for formatting, addressing and error checking, otherwise they could not understand each other's data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark common rules; 1 mark different devices/interoperability. [2]

items.stem: Explain the roles of TCP and IP when a file is sent across the internet.
items.answer: TCP splits the file into numbered packets, checks they arrive and requests resends, then reassembles them in order; IP adds source and destination addresses and routers use them to route each packet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark TCP packets/sequence; 1 mark TCP acknowledgements/resend; 1 mark IP addressing/routing. [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'fibre-optic cable'.
items.answer: A cable that transmits data as pulses of light along thin glass or plastic fibres, giving very high bandwidth over long distances with little interference.

items.stem: Explain why communication via geostationary satellites has noticeable latency.
items.answer: The signal must travel about 35 786 km up to the satellite and the same distance down, which takes around a quarter of a second even at the speed of light.

items.answer: firewall: Hardware or software that monitors traffic between a network and the outside world and blocks or allows packets according to a set of rules. proxy server: A server that acts as an intermediary between users and the internet, forwarding requests, hiding internal addresses, filtering content and caching web pages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: firewall correctly described; 1 mark: proxy server correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'virtual private network (VPN)'.
items.answer: A secure, encrypted connection (tunnel) over a public network such as the internet, allowing a remote user to access a private network as if connected locally.

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'SMTP' and 'TCP/IP'.
items.answer: SMTP: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: used to send emails from a client to a server and between mail servers. TCP/IP: The suite of protocols used by the internet: TCP splits data into packets and ensures reliable, ordered delivery; IP addresses and routes the packets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: SMTP correctly described; 1 mark: TCP/IP correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why protocols are needed for communication on the internet. (b) Explain the roles of TCP and IP when a file is sent across the internet.
items.answer: (a) Devices from different manufacturers and running different software must agree on rules for formatting, addressing and error checking, otherwise they could not understand each other's data. (b) TCP splits the file into numbered packets, checks they arrive and requests resends, then reassembles them in order; IP adds source and destination addresses and routers use them to route each packet.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark common rules; 1 mark different devices/interoperability. [2] (b) 1 mark TCP packets/sequence; 1 mark TCP acknowledgements/resend; 1 mark IP addressing/routing. [3]

items.stem: Silverline Couriers in Auckland runs its own website, email system and internet telephone system. Evaluate whether Silverline Couriers should replace its traditional telephone lines with VoIP.
items.answer: Points for: lower call costs; extra features (video, voicemail to email); works anywhere with internet. Points against / limitations: quality depends on bandwidth; fails in power or internet outages; security of calls; emergency call location. Conclusion: VoIP is usually worthwhile with a reliable connection and a backup line for emergencies.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Against: quality depends on bandwidth; fails in power or internet outages; security of calls; emergency call location. Conclusion may argue: VoIP is usually worthwhile with a reliable connection and a backup line for emergencies. [4]
